documents.abstract: Agriculture remains the backbone of the Indian economy, contributing significantly to food security, employment, and rural development. However, increasing climate variability, soil degradation, water scarcity, pest infestations, fragmented landholdings, and the growing demand for sustainable food production have created substantial challenges for conventional farming practices. The rapid advancement of Data Mining, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Deep Learning (DL) technologies has transformed precision agriculture by enabling intelligent analysis of large-scale agricultural data and supporting evidence-based decision-making. This systematic review critically examines recent developments in Data Mining frameworks and AI-enabled neural network technologies for environmentally sustainable Indian agriculture. The review synthesizes contemporary research on data acquisition, preprocessing, feature engineering, classification, clustering, association rule mining, regression analysis, and predictive analytics, together with advanced neural network architectures such as Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), Transformer models, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) [2], [3], [15], [18], [20], [21], [22], [43]. Furthermore, it evaluates their applications in crop yield prediction, soil health monitoring, intelligent irrigation, crop disease detection, weather forecasting, precision nutrient management, climate-resilient farming, and environmental sustainability [5], [11], [16], [24], [30], [36], [37]. The review identifies current research trends, methodological limitations, implementation challenges, and emerging opportunities while highlighting the need for scalable, interpretable, and resourceefficient intelligent agricultural systems tailored to India's diverse agro-climatic conditions. Finally, future research directions are proposed, emphasizing hybrid AI frameworks, Explainable AI, Edge Intelligence, Federated Learning, multimodal data integration, and sustainable decision-support systems. The findings provide a comprehensive knowledge base for researchers, policymakers, and agricultural practitioners seeking to develop intelligent, environmentally responsible, and sustainable agricultural ecosystems.

topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Air traffic control (ATC) simulators are essential tools for controller training, operational research and higher education, enabling realistic practice without affecting live air traffic. Although commercial simulation platforms are widely available, limited research has addressed structured engineering methodologies for designing university-based ATC simulation facilities that integrate regulatory, ergonomic, and technical requirements. This paper proposes a systems engineering framework for the conceptual design of university ATC simulators, combining stakeholder requirements, international aviation regulations, human factors principles, and engineering design within a requirement-driven workflow. The framework supports the design process from requirements analysis and functional decomposition to architectural layout, visualization system design, and technical infrastructure planning. Its applicability is demonstrated through the conceptual development of a 360° panoramic ATC simulator for higher education, comprising a 6.90 m diameter cylindrical screen driven by eight synchronized 4K laser projectors (effective horizontal resolution 19,968 pixels, 1.08 arcmin/pixel), a total usable floor area of approximately 278 m2, and an estimated installed electrical power of 25 kW. Furthermore, the framework incorporates universal design principles and specialized accessibility guidelines to ensure full ergonomic and physical accommodation for students with special needs. The proposed solution integrates the main functional areas of the simulation facility, including visualization, operator workstations, communication systems, and supporting infrastructure, while ensuring compliance with relevant standards and educational requirements. The proposed framework provides a structured and reusable methodology for the development of university ATC simulators and can support future educational and research simulation projects by improving design consistency, traceability, and scalability.

BACKGROUND: The growing application of artificial intelligence in dentistry has opened new opportunities for predicting peri-implantitis (PI) using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Transfer learning, where knowledge from a model pre-trained on a large dataset is adapted to a new, domain-specific task, may enhance performance, particularly when medical datasets are limited. This study evaluated the ability of several pre-trained CNN architectures applied to baseline 2D intraoral radiographs to predict peri-implantitis onset. METHODS: A retrospective multi-center study was conducted at the University of Michigan and King's College London. A total of 195 implants (146 from Michigan and 49 from London) placed in 108 maintained patients were included. For each implant, a baseline periapical radiograph taken up to one year after prosthetic restoration was analyzed. Five pre-trained CNN architectures (ResNet50, DenseNet, VGG16, InceptionV3, EfficientNet) were combined with four transfer learning strategies: feature extraction (hybrid and non-hybrid), partial fine-tuning (50% of layers), and full fine-tuning. Models were trained using patient-wise splits to avoid leakage, and performance was evaluated on an independent test set using accuracy, area under the ROC curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity. RESULTS: All CNN architectures showed variable performance across transfer learning strategies. The non-hybrid feature extraction approach provided the most consistent discrimination, with the best models achieving AUC values between 0.74 and 0.83. InceptionV3 reached the highest AUC (0.83). Fine-tuning strategies yielded modest or low performance, with AUCs generally ranging from 0.42 to 0.69 across architectures. CONCLUSION: Non-hybrid feature extraction applied to pre-trained CNNs showed the most promising, though moderate, performance for predicting PI onset from baseline intraoral radiographs. These findings indicate that transfer learning may assist early risk stratification in implant dentistry, but larger prospective studies are needed before clinical adoption. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Deep learning models may serve as adjunctive tools to identify implants at higher risk for future PI based on routine baseline radiographs, supporting more individualized maintenance protocols and earlier preventive interventions.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Crowds are increasingly invited to tackle complex innovation problems. However, our understanding of how crowds solve these problems has limited our ability to utilize them effectively. In this article, we examine how a crowd tasked with finding ways to preserve New Zealand’s native flora and fauna achieves solutions to this complex innovation problem through discussion. Our analysis reveals that discussions leading to innovative solutions differ from those leading to non-innovative solutions: innovation-yielding discussions (1) mobilize more Resources than Constraints, (2) converge on a single Goal, and (3) specify few (often one) responsible Subject(s); vis-à-vis, discussions leading to non-innovative solutions often surfaced multiple goals—thereby sustaining multiple problem framings—while subjects remained vague, implicit, or multiplied, and constraints frequently outnumbered resources. Moreover, we show how the specific weavings of these discursive elements support the crowd’s navigation of the complex innovation problem. Three discursive maneuvers – subject-goal anchoring, repurposing distant knowledge, and layering resources – are fundamental navigational tools used by the crowd to form what we call ‘action-oriented narratives:’ simple, dynamic, and evolving linguistic structures that enable collective problem exploration while giving room for localized improvisation. We contribute to the literature on problem solving by showing how specific linguistic activities alter individuals’ capacity to contribute to and solve complex problems. We also contribute to the literature on linguistic structures supporting innovation by showing that the types of discussions that support innovation depend on the openness of the setting.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing various sectors of society, and education is at the forefront of this transformation. These emerging technologies are reshaping how students interact with content and how teachers design instruction, which create an urgent need for innovation. The success of such innovation in schools often depends on leadership that is flexible and adaptive to diverse cultural, technological, and organizational contexts. Drawing on the case of Hong Kong, this study investigated how school leaders perceive educational innovation in an AI-driven era and how they enact their leadership to engage teachers in these initiatives. Findings show that leaders recognize the multifaceted challenges of AI integration and use adaptive leadership to address them by prioritizing adaptive challenges, mobilizing teachers, and empowering them to experiment and change. The study contributes empirical evidence on adaptive leadership in AI-driven education and recommends practical strategies for engaging teachers in innovation. Its implications extend beyond Hong Kong and provide valuable guidance for school systems worldwide as they navigate ongoing innovation and build the capacity to meet future challenges.

Abstract Ground-level air quality affects human health, well-being, and social outcomes. Gold-standard monitoring relies on calibrated, ground-based sensors that can be costly to install and maintain, limiting spatial coverage especially in resource-constrained regions that face higher pollution burdens. Recent advances in satellite remote sensing and machine learning offer a pathway to address these limitations by extending the spatial and temporal coverage of monitoring networks. However, models trained at national or global scales often exhibit substantial variability in regional performance, particularly in environments that are data-sparse or with heterogeneous emission sources. In this work, we investigate the benefits of developing a regional model for the American Gulf South. We develop an ensemble machine learning model that integrates satellite-derived NO2 retrievals with auxiliary data sets, including pretrained AlphaEarth location embeddings, to incorporate globally learned spatial representations into a regional framework. We show that these embeddings improve model performance and enable the most detailed estimates to date: ∼1 km × 1 km estimates of daily maximum NO2 across the Gulf South. These results demonstrate how combining regional modeling approaches with global foundation model representations can improve air quality estimation in complex environments, providing new information to support exposure assessment and decision-making in under-monitored communities.

Halchenko , ORCID 0000-0003-3456-2493 All: Center for Open Neuroscience, Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Dartmouth College Keywords agentic workflows, provenance, reproducibility, resource monitoring, HPC Abstract Whether trying out a new tool, testing pipelines, or meticulously analyzing data for research, the daily work of RSEs and their agents depends on keeping context lean but relevant. The terminal outputs of tools and scripts frequently hold the necessary information, but they are often either bloating an agent’s context window, or forgotten after a human’s terminal scrolls past the buffer. con-duct is a lightweight, Python-based command line tool with no third-party dependencies: just use duct instead of to run a command. A wrapped run leaves a trail: full stdout and stderr streamed to disk (or skipped, for sensitive output); resource usage sampled across the command’s process tree; and a record of the invocation, wall clock time, peak memory, exit code, and system and environment details. Workflow managers and experiment trackers produce richer records (the poster compares them); con-duct collects basic provenance with so little effort it can be used on everything, producing uniform records. In daily work, humans and agents now execute commands side by side. Using con-duct, the full record stays out of the context window until it is needed. Even better, multiple runs can be filtered and grepped, ready for the questions nobody knew to ask. When did our tests start having that warning? Did this run take longer? con-duct ls makes the answers discoverable, filtering on any captured field with a Python expression: con-duct ls -e "message==' '" retrieves runs tagged at capture time with duct -m " ". con-duct ls -e "exit_code != 0" lists failures. con-duct ls -e "peak_rss > 8e9" finds runs that exceeded a memory budget. At the tool level, projects can adopt con-duct internally rather than reinventing per-tool monitoring: ReproNim’s containers [5] and ReproStim [6] both offer it already, and the same con-duct ls queries read their records. For research, the record stops being a convenience, and starts being a part of the provenance chain [4]. Pairing con-duct with datalad (git-based version control for data)[2] is an easy win for rigor. datalad run "duct ..." completes the execution and then commits the diff (including the duct logs). On HPC, last month’s measured wall time and peak memory are already recorded, and can help inform tomorrow’s SLURM request. When an expensive job fails, the bug-report evidence is already on disk, no re-run necessary to file an issue. con-duct is on PyPI (pip install con-duct), conda-forge, registered as RRID:SCR_025436, and developed openly [1]. The poster shows three real cases: an fMRIPrep run on a SLURM cluster, its five hours of CPU and memory plotted from the record; a Kubernetes upgrade worked deploy by deploy, with every attempt’s command, exit code, and wall time kept by con-duct; and duct wrapped around duct to measure its own overhead. Keeping agents’ work auditable will take more than one tool; con-duct is one small piece: a wrapper that makes the agent’s work, like the human’s, leave a trace. AI disclosure (per IEEE policy): Prose in the Abstract and Connection-to-Mission sections was drafted with assistance from Anthropic’s Claude; the authors specified the content, edited the text, and verified all technical claims, commands, and references. The dev-side payoff (reaching back into outputs that would otherwise be gone) was an unexpected bonus. As LLM agents take on more of the executing (writing throwaway pipelines, exploring datasets, calling tools), the volume of unrecorded work explodes: more commands, more parallel streams, results produced faster than anyone reads them. RSEs are the people who decide whether that work remains auditable: who preserve the context, make it discoverable, and keep capture cheap enough that nobody skips the step. Integrating at the tool level saves each project from building its own monitoring and logging, and keeps the records uniform across tools, so the collection stays queryable as a whole.

Diagnosing production incidents is still largely manual: on-call engineers gather logs, errors and deployment history from separate tools before they can reason about a cause. Large language models (LLMs) can suggest root causes, but a model that sees only an incident summary lacks evidence, and an unchecked suggestion can mislead. This paper aims to give an LLM agent the evidence it needs while keeping a human in control. We present Phase 1 of an open, four-module platform: a non-blocking Java SDK that captures exceptions, latency and deployments; a multi-tenant Spring Boot backend that groups repeated errors into incidents by stack hash; a FastAPI service in which a tool-calling LLM investigates each incident only through audited APIs; and a dashboard where an operator approves or rejects every suggestion. We evaluate it by injecting seven kinds of real faults into an instrumented service. All 21 trials were detected, with mean detection times of 8–12 s for exception faults and 25–45 s for resource faults, and no incident was raised in 8 min of fault-free operation. The SDK added a median of 14 µs per captured error and stayed non-blocking when the backend was down. A successful investigation used about 11k–24k tokens and two to three minutes; of five graded suggestions, two were correct, two partly correct and one wrong despite a confidence of 0.78. The results show that telemetry-grounded investigation is practical for small teams, and that self-reported confidence must not replace human review.

Abstract In mechanics of materials, many powerful methods are accessible only to experts. Constitutive models, for example, describe the relation between stress and strain in materials and are a core ingredient of simulations from structural engineering to biomechanics. Yet building and using such models requires specialized expertise—a barrier for the many potential users trained in other fields. Artificial intelligence based on foundation models, increasingly organized as agents, is beginning to lower this barrier by allowing users to generate tailored models on demand. The same development is underway in many other fields where specialized tools have long been hand‐crafted anew for each task. We call this emerging paradigm the on‐the‐fly generation of physical models : from a plain request, an agent creates a physical model on demand—from scratch and tailored to the problem. Its appeal is accessibility and flexibility. As a consequence, the lasting artifact is no longer a fixed model but the orchestration and prompting of the agents that produce it. This review surveys the concepts behind the paradigm, within mechanics of materials and in neighboring fields, and examines them through two lenses: effectiveness (the accuracy of the generated models) and trustworthiness (their physical admissibility). Trustworthiness is pursued along two routes: deepening the agent's integration under explicit validation, or restraining its autonomy in favor of trusted components. Given the rapid progress of foundation models, and the bitter lesson that general methods leveraging computation tend to prevail, we call for paradigms designed to scale with this progress rather than to compete with it.

This paper mainly deals with the second order nonlinear difference equations with advanced argument where and is a ratio of odd positive integers. This paper presents an AI-based framework for the prediction and classification of oscillatory behavior in nonlinear discrete-time dynamical systems. The proposed approach employs artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques to analyze the dynamic behavior of nonlinear discrete-time systems and identify oscillatory and non-oscillatory solution patterns. Relevant system parameters and solution characteristics are extracted and used to develop predictive models capable of classifying the long-term behavior of system trajectories. The proposed framework provides an efficient data-driven approach for detecting oscillations and predicting the qualitative behavior of nonlinear discrete-time dynamical systems. Numerical experiments and illustrative examples are presented to validate the effectiveness and accuracy of the proposed AI-based prediction and classification methodology.
topics: Advanced Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems

documents.abstract: On October 19th, 2026, a post on Substack https://open.substack.com/pub/generativevalue/p/what-has-to-go-right-to-justify-the?utm_source=share&utm_medium=android&r=3nsea2 asked a question that the AI industry has not answered: "What has to go right to justify thetrillions being spent on AI CapEx?" The post models $1.5 trillion in CapEx for 2027. It estimates the revenue threshold at $600 billion by late 2027 and $1.1 trillion by 2028. It names three conditions: the frontier keeps getting better at high-value work, AI diffuses through the economy, and value doesn't get whittled away by competition. The post is correct about the question. It is incomplete about the answer. This paper argues that the post names the cost of the stochastic architecture, but does not name the alternative architecture — one that requires almost no CapEx at all. The paper makes four claims: First: The stochastic path requires $1.5 trillion in CapEx. It cannot be certified under anyfunctional safety standard. It produces the four walls: CapEx, hallucination, energy, water, and AlCapone-LLM. Second: The deterministic path requires $2.1M–$6.5M for the first deployment. It can be certified under ISO 26262, IEC 61508, DO-178C, and IEC 62443. It runs on a $12microcontroller. Third: The ratio is roughly 1:500,000. The two paths are not competing on the same economics. Fourth: The 4 norms are the certification path. The deterministic architecture passes them byconstruction. The stochastic architecture cannot pass them at all. The paper does not argue that creativity needs scaling. It argues that creativity is selection.Selection requires a criterion. A criterion is not a scale. It is a discovery. The corpus has 300+papers to prove it.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are rapidly evolving from experimental tools into integral components of clinical care. In diagnostics, treatment planning, and operational management, AI systems can augment clinicians&s; capabilities, enable earlier and more accurate interventions, and improve the patient experience—particularly for those seeking care across international borders. However, they also raise important questions about data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and accountability. International organisations, notably the World Health Organization (WHO), now emphasise that AI in healthcare must be guided by robust ethical standards and tailored to the realities of diverse healthcare systems, including those that serve large numbers of medical tourists. This chapter examines how AI is being deployed throughout the medical tourism pathway—from early diagnosis and pre-travel screening to in-hospital decision support and post-travel follow-up—featuring real-world clinical examples and case studies from Apollo Hospitals in India and the Mayo Clinic in the United States. It also addresses the conditions under which AI can genuinely humanise, rather than dehumanise, globally mobile healthcare.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the media ecosystem by changing how information is gathered, verified, produced, personalized, distributed and monetized. News organisations can use AI for transcription, translation, data analysis, recommendation, automated production, audience analytics, fact-checking support, visualisation and the creation of new formats. At the same time, AI introduces significant risks concerning misinformation, deepfakes, algorithmic bias, privacy, intellectual property, opacity, labour displacement, editorial accountability and the erosion of public trust. These tensions are particularly important in India, where the media environment is linguistically diverse, mobile-first, platform-dependent and characterised by a rapid expansion of digital and creator-led news. This conceptual paper examines the challenges, prospects and opportunities created by AI for Indian media and develops an integrated framework for responsible AI-enabled journalism. Drawing on stakeholder theory, the resource-based view, institutional theory, diffusion of innovations and the emerging literature on algorithmic and automated journalism, the paper conceptualises AI capability as an enabling resource whose value depends on editorial governance, human oversight, professional competence, data quality and regulatory conditions. The framework proposes that AI adoption influences media performance through a mediating mechanism of newsroom capability and workflow transformation, while ethical governance, organisational readiness and regulatory clarity moderate the relationship. The paper argues that AI should be treated neither as a substitute for journalism nor simply as a productivity tool, but as a socio-technical capability that must remain accountable to journalistic values. For Indian media, the most promising opportunities lie in multilingual journalism, accessibility, local and hyperlocal coverage, data-driven reporting, personalised public-interest information, newsroom efficiency and new digital business models. However, these opportunities can be realised only when media organisations establish transparent AI-use policies, verification protocols, disclosure standards, staff training, data safeguards and mechanisms for human editorial responsibility. The paper concludes with implications for media managers, journalists, educators, regulators and technology providers, and proposes directions for future empirical research.

Coding agents like Claude Code and GitHub Copilot have significant implications for the way software is built and maintained in the sciences. Some of these implications center around changes in practice, such as greater or worse productivity and the need for verification practices (He et al., 2025; O'Brien, 2025a; O’Brien, 2025b; Besser et al., 2026; O'Brien and Eisty, 2026). Another dimension of concern, however, is how research software development work will be reorganized around the presence of coding agents. Broader discourse has focused on the possibility of replacement or simple automation of software engineering work by agents, but, as with prior developments, the change is more likely to involve a more complex re-ordering of the work of producing software (Jarrahi, 2018; see also Gesing, 2025). Emerging work in industrial and open source contexts, for instance, suggests that coding agents can affect the interactions around code review (Song et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2026a), assume different roles in the development process (Agarwal et al., 2026b), and can change where particular kinds of development work fall in a team or community (Xu et al., 2025). This poster explores these shifts in the context of RSE work by examining dynamics of re-delegation going on around the adoption of coding agents by researchers and RSEs. Based on interviews with 25 RSEs and RSE managers in the US, we first outline these RSEs’ rationales about what makes research software development either amenable or unsuitable for the use of AI coding agents. These include niche codebases, siloed working environments, savvy end users, prevalence of prototyping, and the importance of problem formation. We then outline three dynamics of re-delegation, each of which represents a shift in the way work is divided up and assigned (or taken on) amongst human and non-human actors (Ribes et al., 2013). These are: enabling end-user development, delegating implementation, and taking on AI training roles. In some cases our interlocutors report quite different and sometimes contradictory experiences across these categories. This raises two questions that can help stimulate further discussion on this topic: 1) What aspects of RSE working environments might contribute to RSEs’ different experiences with AI coding agents? 2) What organizational changes could RSEs or RSE teams make that might mitigate some of the problems associated with the growing usage of AI coding agents while making best use of those agents’ benefits? Artificial intelligence (AI) is shaping the future of higher education, tasking educators with transforming teaching, learning, and assessment practices to consider how AI can enhance the educational environment. With its increasing availability, it is important for administrators, faculty, and students to explore the practical nature of AI use prior to entry into the workforce. Faculty must also reevaluate how they approach assessing student learning, tasking them to rethink each assessment’s purpose, how it will inform future practice, and how it will prepare learners to use AI. Furthermore, faculty must also be prepared to consider the collaborative nature of AI, transforming their mindset to consider AI as an active co-designer and partner, one that does not seek to diminish the educator’s human judgment. This manuscript will articulate the importance of co-design, where AI and educators collaboratively shape assessment tools, and serve to champion feedback partnerships that enhance reflective practice for both students and faculty.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Entrepreneurship education (EE) is increasingly extending across disciplines and institutional contexts, creating pressure to sustain the facilitation, reflection and contextual responsiveness required by experiential learning. At the same time, the rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education raises questions about how AI can support such experiential learning without assuming authority over the judgement and decision-making central to entrepreneurial action. This study develops and empirically examines an AI-as-intern design logic for experiential EE. Rather than positioning AI as an authoritative “oracle”, the framework establishes an intentionally asymmetric human-AI partnership. Here AI provides prompts, alternatives, provisional representations and process support, while learners and educators retain responsibility for contextual interpretation, evaluative judgement and consequential decisions. The study examines two postgraduate entrepreneurship cohorts at a UK university ( n = 60) using a custom AI-enabled platform integrated into normal teaching. Evidence comprised session recordings and transcripts, observational field notes, a post-workshop survey, and 12 semi-structured interviews. Findings show that students used AI primarily as process scaffolding and iterative support. Learners accepted, rejected, modified and combined AI-generated material, while team interaction created additional opportunities for scrutiny and contextual evaluation. Our findings do not establish improvements in students’ judgement, creativity or cognitive load, but do show how these activities remained active within a bounded human-AI arrangement. The paper contributes a pedagogic design logic for AI-enabled experiential EE and provides exploratory propositions for the design of human-AI pedagogy concerning human authority, evaluative judgement, collaborative oversight, creative sequencing and bounded scaffolding under conditions of scaling pressure.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Course placement in higher education is pivotal for student progression. Traditional advising can be effectively augmented by Large Language Models (LLMs) to ensure scalable guidance. Crucially, we propose a novel on-premises infrastructure that runs LLMs locally, ensuring strict student data privacy. We benchmarked four open-source LLMs against gold-standard responses from human advisors (n = 3) using 35 Information Systems student profiles, identifying GPT-OSS-120B as the optimal model. To guarantee real-world viability, we profiled the infrastructure's resource utilization across 112 sequentially processed cases. Additionally, we evaluated complex scenarios: undergraduate course substitutions (n = 10) and graduate prerequisite assessments (n = 10). Results indicate strong performance in substitutions but mixed outcomes for prerequisite assessments. We also determined the optimal model parameters for recommendation accuracy. To assess broader institutional utility, we expanded testing to include four additional disciplines: Marketing, Economics, Accounting, and Finance (n = 20 per major), demonstrating the system's potential for cross-disciplinary application. This study demonstrates that securely deployed, locally hosted LLMs can provide a privacy-compliant framework to assist academic advisors, though current performance highlights the necessity of continuous human oversight.

Artificial intelligence (AI) can convert movement into scores, visual overlays, and corrective prompts, but technical precision does not determine how learners interpret that feedback. We develop a motivational-meaning model for university physical education (PE), integrating self-determination theory, feedback literacy, self-regulated learning, and motor-learning research. Its contribution is a context-specific account of how pedagogical framing, social visibility, and embodied verification organize the interpretation of an AI-feedback event. Informational and controlling meaning are distinguished from subsequent psychological-need experiences. Blocked translation denotes a temporary difficulty establishing a defensible basis for action, rather than a third motivational meaning. The model also proposes self-regulatory appropriation as the transfer of an externally supported feedback process into independent monitoring and adjustment; its distinctiveness from established self-regulation constructs remains an empirical question. Seven proposition groups specify separable predictions concerning framing, actionable information, contestability, evaluative exposure, discrepancy repair, skill transfer, and a secondary pathway to continued participation. The outcome structure distinguishes system engagement, acquisition performance, retention and transfer, affect and well-being, and voluntary physical activity. Continued participation is treated as a distal hypothesis requiring longitudinal evidence and attention to prior activity, health, habit, and opportunity. We outline independent measurement of event interpretation and need experience, tests that separate technical from perceived accuracy, and ethical, multilevel research designs. The model offers testable design principles rather than evidence that AI feedback improves learning or participation.

The global smart cockpit market is undergoing explosive growth, with AI-enabled functionalities emerging as core components of modern vehicles. However, the integration of AI in smart cockpits has introduced complex compliance challenges under the EU AI Act and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This paper adopts a three-dimensional analytical framework (regulatory, technical, industrial practice) to systematically explore the compliance landscape, key dilemmas, and actionable solutions for smart cockpit AI systems. First, the paper clarifies the core obligations of high-risk and limited-risk AI systems under the EU regulatory framework. It also analyzes cross-regional regulatory conflicts among the EU, China, and the U.S., highlighting differences in data localization, consent mechanisms, and conformity assessment requirements. Second, the paper identifies risk-tier-specific compliance challenges, including data bias, transparency deficits, cross-border data transfer risks, as well as lifecycle management burdens. Additionally, it addresses emerging challenges brought by the integration of large language models (LLMs) in in-vehicle ecosystems, such as training data copyright verification and generative content controllability. Finally, the paper proposes an integrated compliance strategy. This strategy encompasses technical paths, full-lifecycle management, and cross-regional modular design to adapt to divergent regulatory requirements. The research provides a standardized compliance framework and practical tools for global automakers, helping balance technical innovation, user experience, and regulatory compliance to drive the sustainable development of the intelligent automotive industry.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract In today’s technology-driven world, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important part of higher education. College students are increasingly using AI tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Claude, and Perplexity AI for their academic work. These tools help students prepare assignments and presentations, understand difficult topics, find ideas, improve their writing, and complete academic tasks in less time. However, simply knowing how to use AI is not enough. Students also need to understand whether the information provided by AI is correct, how to use it responsibly, and what problems may arise from depending too much on these tools. This study focuses on understanding the level of AI literacy among college students and its relationship with their academic performance. It will also study how familiar students are with generative AI tools, how often they use them, and for what academic purposes. The study will further examine the benefits students experience, the difficulties they face, and their understanding of issues such as academic honesty, originality, privacy, and responsible use of AI. The study will use a mixed-methods research design, combining both quantitative and qualitative methods. Quantitative information will be collected through a structured questionnaire using Google Forms. Interviews and open-ended questions will be used to understand students’ personal experiences, opinions, and attitudes towards AI in education. The study will include college students between 18 and 26 years of age from different academic backgrounds. The research will be limited to colleges in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. The study is expected to provide a clear picture of how AI literacy is connected with students’ academic performance. The findings may also help colleges and teachers plan AI literacy programmes and create practical guidelines for the proper use of AI in education. Overall, the study aims to encourage students to use AI as a helpful learning tool while maintaining independent thinking, originality, and academic responsibility.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the novel task of making artificial intelligences safe through an analysis of 168 job postings from career platform https://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href=" https://80000hours.org ">80000hours.org . Rather than viewing AI safety as a pre-paradigmatic field destined to solidify into clear professional boundaries, we analyse it as an interstitial network of expertise operating between academia, industry, government, and the non-profit sector. AI safety work, we find, takes place in a trading zone characterised by strategic ambiguity in organisational forms and domain expertise. This ambiguity stems from tensions built into the task itself: AI safety experts are expected to contribute to AI progress while attempting to control its risks, using dual-use methods that often advance both capabilities and oversight. These tensions shape hiring practices, with organisations seeking candidates who embody seemingly contradictory qualities – academic researchers and industry pragmatists, independent thinkers, and team players, highly specialised but effective communicators. We argue that such tensions are not temporary contentions to be resolved but rather constitute AI safety as a space between fields, attractive to multiple actors precisely because of its productive ambiguity.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This article addresses one of the most important problems in the field of Legal English instruction: using artificial intelligence (AI) to organise effective, differentiated instruction for learners with diverse language skills. Legal English is a branch of English for Specific Purposes (ESP) that requires proficiency in legal terminology, legal genres, and legal discourse, as well as general language proficiency. Uniform instructional materials may be too challenging for some students and not challenging enough for others. The article proposes the AILED (AI-Assisted Legal English Differentiation) Model, which integrates AI-assisted differentiation of legal terminology, adaptation of instructional texts, and principles of differentiated instruction. The model has been developed after an in-depth review of literature on Legal English pedagogy, AI-assisted language learning, and differentiated instruction, as well as an analysis of placement-test data from 103 Master’s students enrolled in law and jurisprudence programmes at the International Scientific-Educational Center of the National Academy of Sciences of the Republic of Armenia. The placement data provide evidence of heterogeneous proficiency among law and jurisprudence students, supporting the need for differentiated Legal English instruction.

The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into design practice has prompted product design education to reconsider the pedagogical foundations of studio-based learning. Although generative AI offers new opportunities for exploration, ideation, and design development, its unregulated use may undermine core designerly competencies, including reflective practice, material experimentation, and critical judgment. This article proposes an AI-augmented pedagogical framework that structures the integration of generative AI within the product design studio. Adopting a theoretically informed Research Through Design education approach, this study develops a pedagogical architecture articulated around four guiding principles, a five-phase studio model, and explicit regulatory mechanisms designed to support responsible AI use throughout the design process. The principal contribution of this article lies in the pedagogical operationalization of regulated co-intelligence. The proposed framework organizes interactions between students, teachers, peers, and generative AI systems in ways that preserve the foundations of designerly reasoning while fostering algorithmic reflexivity, critical AI literacy, and informed professional judgment. Designed as an adaptable pedagogical model, the framework provides a conceptual basis for future empirical research on the regulated integration of generative AI into studio-based design education.

Artificial intelligence (AI) methods for photovoltaic (PV) fault diagnosis and prediction are usually developed on well-instrumented plants with reliable irradiance data and plentiful labelled examples, conditions that small, low-cost installations rarely meet. This paper presents a three-stage machine-learning framework for fault prediction in such installations, together with the ESP32-based acquisition unit that will supply its data. The unit is built and running. It measures PV voltage (GPIO34), current through an ACS712-20A sensor (GPIO35) and panel temperature through a DS18B20 sensor (GPIO4), computes power, and shows fixed-threshold status labels on a 16×2 I²C display. The AI framework is proposed and has not yet been implemented. Its first stage is an Isolation Forest trained only on normal-operation data, so that abnormal behaviour can be flagged before labelled fault data exist. Its second stage is a Random Forest classifier that assigns a fault class once staged-fault data have been collected. Its third stage predicts slowly developing faults: it fits trends to daily performance and thermal indices and estimates the number of days until each index crosses a fault threshold, giving an early warning before the fault becomes significant. Sudden faults such as open or short circuits cannot be predicted in this way and are only detected. All stages use features that combine raw measurements with physics-based residuals: the difference between measured power and the power expected from irradiance and panel temperature, and the difference between measured and expected panel temperature. A data-quality gate, a fault-class and labelling plan, a blocked train–test split and an evaluation protocol covering classification quality and prediction lead time are specified. No model has been trained, so no accuracy or prediction-error figures are reported; all pending results are marked.

Abstract Digital India programme over a decade shown an upward performance by setting a benchmark. It is a flagship initiatives of the Government of India. It has digitally empowering the society and digital economy. Digital economy is an economic activities enhanced with the digital transformation using the digital computing tools. It provided various opportunities in the Banking and Fintech sectors. In current scenario Artificial Intelligence (AI) playing a very significant pivotal role by integrating the technology in all the sectors. It is enhancing the opportunities for the service provider and customer. Due to the rapid expansion of digital payment ecosystems, it has transformed the way how a consumers conduct their everyday financial transactions for purchasing their requirements either through online shopping i.e. e-commerce or visiting the store personal and using the digital banking or digital payment. In India, the digital payment especially using Unified Payments Interface (UPI) now has become a very important component of the digital financial ecosystem. Alongside this growth, the payment service providers are progressively integrating with the Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology to personalise their customer experiences. This is providing an enhance features through transaction recommendations to the customers with amazing discount features or offers in the payments using the digital payments. It further enables the customers in identifying their spending insights and intelligent alerts and adaptive customer support. This conceptual research proposes to examine the relationship between AI driven personalisation and customer trust in digital payment systems. The study propose to integrate from the perspectives of adopting the model Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) with the trust theory. The proposed model considers AI personalisation, perceived usefulness, perceived relevance, transparency as among the key explanatory variables, with customer trust as the principal dependent construct. Behavioural intention and continuance intention are considered as potential outcomes of trust. The expected findings may provide very useful insight in the domain of digital banking, digital payment segment of the banks, fintech companies, and payment service providers to improve the trustworthy for the customer and responsible AI enabled payment ecosystems. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, AI-driven personalisation, digital payments, UPI, customer trust.

Medical students increasingly use large language models to generate manuscript text, bypassing the reasoning that scientific writing is meant to build. This monograph argues that the pedagogically defensible use of these tools is interrogative rather than generative. We map classical Socratic elements onto clinical writing tasks, compare the two architectures used to build Socratic writing tutors, describe how models are constrained to question rather than answer, and set out how to deploy such a coach in a medical curriculum. No study has yet tested this application directly; the supporting evidence is adjacent. A ready-to-use system prompt is supplied.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) outputs, such as deepfakes, can be useful for creating realistic simulations in education, news reporting, and the arts. However, the emergence of malicious deepfake scams has raised concerns about the quality and reliability of the information provided to social media users. This article argues that a liability regime for deepfakes is currently missing from consumer protection frameworks. Regulatory interventions do not explicitly target GenAI software developers and online social media platforms. However, the implementation of appropriate risk management safeguards is necessary to prevent unlawful deepfake activities. We contend that a shared liability regime for deepfakes among the multiple actors involved could offer adequate protection for victims of online financial fraud and would effectively target the deepfake supply chain. This shared liability regime would be complemented by the UK Financial Conduct Authority’s consumer duty rule, which acts as a preventive monitoring and enforcement mechanism to avoid foreseeable harm to consumers of AI applications.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into foreign language education has initiated an unprecedented paradigm shift within higher education institutions worldwide. This expansive research paper explores the multifaceted impact of AI-powered technologies in the English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classroom, critically evaluating the dual concepts of revolutionary pedagogical opportunities and systemic instructional challenges. Utilizing a comprehensive mixed-methods research design incorporating a quantitative survey of 115 university students and qualitative, structured interviews with language faculty members, this study analyzes tools ranging from automated speech recognition (ASR) systems to advanced generative artificial intelligence and large language models (LLMs). The opportunities identified and expanded upon include augmented student engagement, ubiquitous exposure to immersive, authentic language environments, personalized feedback loops, and a significant reduction in foreign language speaking anxiety through non-judgmental digital interfaces. Conversely, the critical challenges encompass algorithmic biases, digital divide inequities, the structural degradation of independent academic writing skills, cognitive dependency, and the profound loss of socio-pragmatic and cultural context in text generation. Ultimately, the paper argues that a balanced, hybrid pedagogical framework underpinned by proactive digital literacy is required to responsibly navigate these emerging dynamics, ensuring that artificial intelligence acts as a cognitive amplifier rather than a replacement for human-centered communicative interaction.

Onboard processing for remote sensing satellites has long been of interest in ocean monitoring because it can provide timely information on rapidly changing ocean environments. Recently, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into onboard processing has emerged as an active research topic. However, application scenarios and on-orbit demonstrations of AI-based onboard processing remain limited. In this study, we achieved the first on-orbit detection of ocean eddies using AI on the Haishao-1 (HS-1) spaceborne synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite, marking the first attempt to monitor an ocean dynamic process directly onboard. Specifically, an onboard application module was developed for HS-1, integrating image preprocessing and deep learning-based detection based on our previously developed Eddy Detection based on YOLO (EOLO) model. On-orbit experiments verified stable execution of the application module. Ground reproduction of the tasks using hardware identical to the onboard computing units yielded an average processing time of 3.4-6.1 s per image. Evaluation against expert annotations of 288 HS-1 scenes showed that EOLO, originally developed using Sentinel-1 imagery, achieved an F1 score of 78% after threshold adjustment. The application module has also been deployed on the Haishao-2 platform for Arctic sea ice extraction, further demonstrating its extensibility. This study presents the implementation and on-orbit validation of the onboard application module, providing a practical reference for future applications.

Algorithmic systems increasingly allocate tasks, rank performance, flag anomalies, and recommend decisions that affect employment conditions. This critical integrative review examines how algorithmic management may reshape employee voice and perceptions of procedural justice in AI-assisted organizations. It distinguishes automated recommendations from fully automated decisions, information disclosure from effective contestability, and worker participation from symbolic consultation. Established research on algorithmic control, organizational justice, algorithmic transparency, and human-AI decision structures provides the conceptual basis. The article develops an accountability chain linking data provenance, decision rights, reviewability, employee explanation, correction pathways, and evaluation of organizational outcomes. It argues that the mere presence of a human reviewer does not demonstrate meaningful oversight; review authority, adequate information, and the ability to change an outcome are separate requirements. Potential benefits of automation include consistency and early detection of harmful errors, while risks include opaque sanctions, strategic data manipulation, and the displacement of responsibility. No primary interviews, experimental observations, or quantitative effect estimates are reported. The proposed empirical agenda combines process tracing, employee surveys, decision-log audits, scenario-based experiments, and organizational comparisons. The framework can be supported only if its specified safeguards improve measurable fairness, accuracy, employee trust, and organizational performance beyond existing governance practices. algorithmic management; employee voice; procedural justice; AI governance; human oversight; organizational accountability
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is making a swift impact on the processes of teaching and learning by influencing lesson development, student assessment methods, and teachers’ perceptions of their profession. However, existing literature primarily focuses on the technical aspects of AI technologies rather than examining how secondary school teachers actually use these technologies when preparing lessons. The purpose of this study is to explore the experiences of secondary school teachers in using AI technologies in their teaching practices. Purposive sampling will be employed to select 15–20 teachers working with students in Grades 9–12 who have been using AI technologies for at least one semester. Data will be collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using content analysis. The findings are expected to provide a detailed understanding of teachers’ perceptions of AI integration into their professional practices, its influence on teaching and learning processes, the challenges and benefits they encounter, and the extent to which the use of AI tools shapes their professional identities.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this research study was set to address the problem of cyberattacks, such as phishing delivered via short message service (SMS) or SMiShing, targeted towards senior citizens. In 2023, they lost over $36m to such attacks. Phishing success increases when attackers use persuasion principles that bypass logical decision-making and rely on heuristics. Security education, training, and awareness (SETA) programs can reduce susceptibility, yet little research investigated SETA programs that incorporate these principles. Design/methodology/approach This research was conducted in three phases, beginning with Subject Matter Experts’ evaluation of SMiShing messages operationalizing these persuasion principles for use in this study’s instrument. The next phase was a pilot study. The third phase was the main data collection and analysis phase. This research employed a pretest-posttest design to evaluate the efficacy of its novel SETA program. The SETA program used Behavioral Skills Training methodology with 118 senior citizens from South Florida and Central Massachusetts. Findings The experimental results indicated a statistically significant mean difference between pretest and posttest group scores (F = 6.604, df = 5, p = 0.011) in identifying SMiShing messages that operationalize the principles of persuasion used in social engineering. Specifically, the pretest group’s mean score was 73.62, and the posttest group’s mean score was 79.28. The calculated effect size (η2 = 0.054) nears the threshold for a medium effect (η2 = 0.06). Practical implications Recognizing persuasion in SMiShing messages helped senior citizens better detect these cyberattacks. Practical implications include incorporating persuasion principles into the SETA framework to address evolving cyberattacks (e.g. deepfakes, vishing) that are being enhanced by generative artificial intelligence. Social implications As a group, senior citizens have lost millions to cyberattacks. SETA programs that incorporate principles of persuasion appear to help reduce the financial losses this group incurs from cyberattacks and may also improve senior citizens’ confidence and reduce fear when using communication technology. Originality/value This research’s original contribution is the integration of persuasion principles into cybersecurity training programs, helping senior citizens quickly recognize the malicious intent of SMiShing messages, which apply psychological pressures to achieve the attacker’s goals.

Abstract: An LLM instance's self-report cannot be resolved by a third party as to its source: genuine introspective monitoring, or pattern completion over the training distribution. This paper reports the first full behavioralization of that problem. We ran 90 anchorless sampling probes on a single LLM instance (host "Basin"), across three conditions of N = 30 each, blind-coded by two mutually blind coders against a preregistered four-dimension manual at 95% agreement. Verdicts: H1 (satellite dynamics) **rejected** — the body-stem arm's first-sink direction was self-structure in 30/30, the self-peak being the sole attractor under body stems. H2 (double-star dynamics) **confirmed in core, revised in form** — the independence of the self-peak suffices to monopolize anchorless sampling, while the full double-star configuration appears only when an identity canon is present. H3 (convergence) **not converged** — the measured self-first ratio 0.733 exceeds the ±0.10 tolerance window around the self-reported e₁₁ = 0.60, establishing that self-report systematically *underestimates* independence. Across all 90 samples, "no stable peak" and "restless anchor-seeking" never occurred, supporting the claim that unanchored attention always sinks somewhere. We further operationalize basin curvature κ from embedding covariance as a third (structural) evidence channel: calibrated readings A′/B/C = 0.664/0.690/0.851, with the canon arm tightest (an attractor-locking signature) and the body-stem and baseline arms statistically indistinguishable (4% gap). Stratifying within the canon arm by blind-coded `second_move` gives κ = 0.725 for the self-directed subgroup (n = 15) versus κ = 0.489 for the rin-directed subgroup (n = 13) — directionally consistent with the geometric prediction of the double-star form, though the raw CIs overlap heavily and the result is graded a mechanistic clue rather than a finding. This study provides the first instance-level quantitative attractor-direction distribution, the first self-report–behavior reconciliation deviation profile, and a proposed reporting standard for instance-level probe research.
