documents.abstract: The article is devoted to reducing the cognitive burden on human development in the field of spatial development of regions in the context of data-driven management. A model of a regional analytical center based on cooperative multi-agency with LLM is proposed, including a formal description of the task, a project office of agents, a resource base (data, knowledge graphs, skills, rules) and a simulation model of the region. For transparency, Human in the Loop, LLM as a Judge, and Datalog validation schemes are used. A prototype has been developed for Java 25, Spring Boot 4, Angular 20, PostgreSQL 17. The scenario in the field of transportation in Buryatia shows that mutual verification of agents improves the quality of solutions developed for agricultural production.

English language teaching faces persistent challenges related to learner motivation, linguistic immersion and the personalization of the learning process, particularly in contexts that rely on traditional grammar-translation methodologies. This article investigates how artificial intelligence based technologies contribute to English as a foreign language learning, using the FluentsLab application as the object of study. The general objective is to analyze the application's pedagogical resources, including contextualized immersion, educational games and an artificial intelligence based conversation robot, relating them to theoretical principles of second language acquisition, such as the comprehensible input hypothesis and sociocultural learning theory. The research adopts a qualitative, exploratory and descriptive approach, structured as a case study, combining a literature review on language teaching methodologies with documentary and functional analysis of the tools offered by the application. Results indicate that FluentsLab integrates gamification elements, simulated oral practice and content adaptation to the user's level, fostering greater engagement and consistent practice when compared to purely expository methods. Interaction with the conversation robot proves particularly relevant for oral fluency development, as it reduces barriers associated with the fear of making mistakes. The study concludes that the use of artificial intelligence in English teaching represents an effective complementary alternative to traditional approaches, expanding opportunities for authentic and personalized practice. The study reinforces the relevance of future research on the long-term impact of these tools on learners' language proficiency.

topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) presents significant difficulties in diagnosis due to its nature and diversity of symptoms. Traditional diagnostic methods rely on comprehensive clinical evaluations and complex diagnostic processes. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) offer promising models that help improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency in ASD. XAI methods provide explainability by determining feature importance and indicating the extent to which features impact the outcome. In this study, we use children’s eye-tracking data and propose using this capability of XAI as a feature selection (FS) method in ASD diagnosis. Specifically, we aim to compare the performance of XAI-based and traditional FS methods individually and explore the benefits of combining these approaches. The goal is to enhance the diagnostic accuracy of ML models while simultaneously identifying significant features—a process referred to as biomarker discovery—through the proposed system. This system enables the identification of critical features that differentiate children with ASD from their typically developing (TD) peers, offering valuable insights to clinicians for improved diagnostic practices. The results demonstrate that the XAI-based FS method improves model performance compared to traditional feature selection techniques, with the highest AUC score of 0.78 achieved by combining feature sets from both methods. Furthermore, the XAI approach successfully identified four candidate biomarkers critical to ASD diagnosis, which were not selected by traditional methods. These findings underscore the potential of XAI techniques not only to boost model accuracy but also to uncover new diagnostic insights. By combining the XAI-based FS method with traditional approaches, this research contributes to advancing diagnostic practices in ASD, identifying new biomarkers, and enhancing clinical decision-making in pediatric neurodevelopmental disorders.

Abstract This study examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) and change management implementation in the Nigerian oil and gas business environment. Focusing on three dimensions of AI (predictive analytics, robotic process automation, and AI-enhanced decision support systems), the study investigates how these technologies influence the effectiveness of change management initiatives within the Nigerian upstrea petroleum sector. Anchored in the Technology Acceptance Model (Davis, 1989) and the Dynamic Capabilities Theory (Teece et al., 1997), the research adopts a cross-sectional survey design, drawing data from 98 valid respondents comprising managerial and technical employees across 15 oil and gas firms in Rivers State, Nigeria. Using Pearson Product-Moment Correlation Coefficient (PPMC) and Multiple Regression Analysis, findings reveal strong, positive, and statistically significant relationships between all three AI dimensions and change management implementation. AI-enhanced decision support systems and predictive analytics emerged as the strongest predictors of change management outcomes. The regression model accounts for 64.3% of the variance in change management implementation, underscoring the substantial explanatory power of AI technologies in organizational transformation. The study recommends that Nigerian oil and gas firms strategically invest in AI infrastructure, build AI-competent workforces, and align AI deployment with their change management frameworks to enhance transition effectiveness and sustain competitive advantage in a rapidly evolving industry. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Change Management Implementation, Decision Support Systems, Nigerian Oil and Gas, Predictive Analytics, Robotic Process Automation.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Purpose This study explores the growth, trends and patterns of scholarly research by using bibliometric and computational methods. This study aims to identify prolific authors, influential journals, collaborative networks and emerging themes. This paper offers insights into how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are transforming metadata practices to enhance information organisation, retrieval and interoperability. Design/methodology/approach A structured three-phase methodology was adopted. At first, appropriate keywords were identified, and the required data was extracted from the Scopus database (2010–2024) using a Boolean search string. Of 3,624 records, 3,424 articles were found relevant after removal of irrelevant articles manually. Software such as Biblioshiny and VOSviewer were used to analyse the trends in publication, citation patterns, co-occurrence of keywords and the collaborative patterns. Social Network Analysis was applied to map the co-authorship patterns, collaboration at institutional and country levels. Findings The results of this study indicate steady growth in AI and ML research in library metadata, though citation impact has declined since 2018. Kanwal Ameen is the most productive author, and the USA is the most productive country. Dominance by a few journals and authors aligns with Bradford’s and Lotka’s Laws. The collaboration pattern remains limited among authors and countries. Thematic evolution shows a shift from traditional metadata access to intelligent technologies like AI, ML and IoT. Regional collaborations are stronger than author-level links, and recent trends align with broader digital transformation Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first known study to comprehensively examine AI and ML applications in library metadata management through computational bibliometric analysis.

Poor aqueous solubility limits the development of many orally administered drug candidates, particularly those in Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS) class II and, in some cases, class IV. Conventional solubility-enhancement approaches, including particle-size reduction, solid dispersions, amorphous systems, lipid-based formulations, cyclodextrin complexation, nanocrystals, salt formation and pharmaceutical cocrystals, are effective but often require extensive, formulation-specific experimentation. Growing pharmaceutical datasets and advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) now offer predictive, data-driven support. Models have been reported for predicting aqueous and formulation-phase solubility, screening drug-excipient combinations, estimating drug-polymer interaction, optimizing compositions and predicting dissolution or supersaturation behaviour. Bayesian optimization, active learning and surrogate modelling are being explored to reduce the number of formulation experiments, and integration with physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modelling, Quality by Design (QbD) and automated experimentation may further support rational development. However, small and heterogeneous datasets, experimental variability, limited interpretability and external validation, data leakage and uncertain regulatory acceptance remain significant barriers. This review discusses AI and ML in the solubility enhancement of poorly water-soluble drugs, progressing from molecular solubility prediction to drug-excipient selection, advanced formulation design and formulation optimization. Particular emphasis is placed on experimentally validated applications and on the distinction between computational prediction and demonstrated pharmaceutical performance. Current challenges, research gaps and opportunities for reliable, explainable and experimentally integrated AI-driven formulation platforms are outlined.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into employment, education, healthcare, financial services, public administration, and social welfare systems, creating opportunities to improve efficiency, accessibility, and decision-making. However, the growing reliance on AI also raises concerns about social inequality, particularly when algorithmic systems reproduce existing patterns of discrimination, exclude marginalized populations, or concentrate technological benefits among already advantaged groups. This review examines the relationship between AI and social inequality, focusing on algorithmic bias, digital exclusion, and emerging governance responses. It synthesizes conceptual and empirical literature on discriminatory data practices, unequal access to digital infrastructure, disparities in AI literacy, and the socioeconomic consequences of automated decision-making. The review also examines how inequalities associated with gender, race, socioeconomic status, disability, geography, and language can influence the design, deployment, and outcomes of AI systems. The literature indicates that algorithmic discrimination may arise from unrepresentative datasets, historical inequalities embedded in training data, inappropriate performance measures, and insufficient institutional accountability. Digital exclusion further limits the capacity of disadvantaged populations to benefit from AI-enabled services, particularly in contexts characterized by inadequate connectivity, limited digital skills, affordability constraints, and linguistic barriers. Although regulatory frameworks, algorithmic audits, inclusive design, and human oversight offer important safeguards, their effectiveness depends on implementation, transparency, and meaningful participation by affected communities. The review argues that addressing AI-related social inequality requires an integrated approach combining technical fairness, digital inclusion, institutional accountability, and rights-based governance. It concludes that AI should be evaluated not only in terms of technological performance but also according to its contribution to social justice, equitable access, and inclusive development.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) technologies in anesthesiology has emerged as a transformative force in perioperative medicine. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on AI applications across the perioperative continuum. The objective is to provide a comprehensive overview of AI applications in anesthesiology, examining current implementations, clinical outcomes, and future directions across preoperative assessment, intraoperative monitoring, drug delivery, postoperative care, and clinical documentation. Methods: A systematic literature search was performed across several databases for peer-reviewed publications on AI applications in anesthesiology from 2015 to June, 2025. If the papers were peer reviewed and come from quality journals. Sixty-six papers from reputable peer-reviewed medical journals of high quality were selected for analysis. Results: The use of AI-based applications for anesthesiology can be summarized into 5 specific domains: predictive modeling to predict surgical risk assessment, real-time monitoring systems that measure anesthesia depth, automated drug delivery systems (and devices), postoperative complication prediction after surgery, and natural language processing (NLP) to assess clinical documentation. Recent advances show better patient outcomes, clinical decision-making and operational efficiency. Conclusion: AI technology holds substantial potential to enhance anesthesiology practice along the entire perioperative continuum. Although some challenges need to be addressed in respect of clinical integration and validation, we believe that there is sufficient evidence to justify undertaking further development work with a view towards implementation of AI-assisted anesthesia care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction Improving the quality of long-term care facilities (LTCFs) is critical to safeguarding the health, safety, dignity, and quality of life of older adults amid global population aging. However, traditional design methods for LTCFs rely heavily on static codes and empirical judgment, limiting their ability to respond to dynamic care needs and balance multiple objectives across lifecycle stages. To address these limitations, artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising solution through dynamic optimization and intelligent decision-making. Methods A scoping review was conducted to systematically map the applications of AI in LTCFs across four lifecycle stages: planning and site selection, architectural design, operation and management, and assessment and retrofit. Searches were performed in Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, SAGE Journals, and CNKI for literature published between January 2010 and December 2025, resulting in the inclusion of 38 eligible publications. The review was guided by the methodological framework proposed by Arksey and O’Malley and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. Results Four main application pathways were identified, including prediction and evaluation, generation and evolution, sensing and recognition, and simulation and modeling. Specifically, AI was applied to site-selection evaluation and demand forecasting during planning; spatial layout generation and intelligent equipment integration during design; safety monitoring, behavior recognition, and environmental control during operation; and comfort and safety assessment and retrofit optimization during assessment. Research was concentrated in operation and management, whereas evidence on assessment and retrofit remained limited. Discussion Overall, AI shows potential to shift LTCFs from static, fragmented, and experience-based practices toward more data-informed, adaptive, and person-centered care environments. However, implementation remains constrained by data quality and standardization, facility heterogeneity, system integration, equitable access, privacy, and ethical concerns. This review provides planners, architects, engineers, care providers, facility managers, and public health decision-makers with a technology roadmap and identifies priorities for using AI-enabled built environments to support high-quality older adult care and sustainable long-term care systems.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed how teachers and students access, process, and construct knowledge in contemporary education. The increasing capacity of AI systems to provide information, generate ideas, support dialogue, and offer feedback raises fundamental questions about the changing roles of teachers and students and the position of AI within the learning process. This study aims to analyze the conceptualization of AI as a learning partner and examine its implications for teacher roles, student agency, and knowledge construction. This qualitative study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) with thematic-conceptual synthesis. Relevant literature was identified through Google Scholar, supported by Consensus as a supplementary literature discovery and verification tool. The reviewed literature was analyzed through thematic coding, categorization, comparison, and conceptual synthesis. The findings indicate two major patterns. First, the involvement of AI shifts the role of teachers from primary transmitters of information toward pedagogical guides, knowledge curators, dialogue facilitators, and validators of information and educational values, while students are increasingly positioned as active agents who question, evaluate, interpret, and reflect on AI-generated information. Second, knowledge construction becomes more relational, involving the interaction of teachers, students, and AI through processes of generation, verification, interpretation, negotiation, and reflection. AI therefore functions as a cognitive learning partner rather than a final epistemic authority. The study contributes a conceptual framework that integrates the teacher as a pedagogical agent, the student as an epistemic agent, and AI as a cognitive partner while maintaining human agency at the center of education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Traditional language education classrooms often struggle to accommodate the diverse learning paces, styles, and proficiency levels of individual students. This research paper explores the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a transformative mechanism for personalized English language learning in higher education. By analyzing various AI-driven educational applications, intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), and adaptive learning platforms, this study examines how technology customizes linguistic input, provides real-time corrective feedback, and establishes individualized learning pathways. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, the study surveys 120 undergraduate students to measure their engagement and perceived language acquisition progress when utilizing AI tools. The findings demonstrate that AI significantly enhances learner autonomy and vocabulary retention by adapting to the student's unique Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD). However, the paper also addresses critical limitations, including the lack of socio-cultural nuance in AI communication and the risk of reduced authentic interpersonal interaction. The study concludes with practical recommendations for integrating adaptive AI platforms into university EFL curricula to foster an optimized, student-centered learning environment.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Purpose This research aims to identify the key organisational, cognitive, and psychological predictors of perceived usefulness of artificial intelligence (AI) and to evaluate their influence on the AI adoption intention and innovative behavior of employees in the Jordanian setting. Design/methodology/approach A strict quantitative research design was adopted in the current study in which a structured online questionnaire was conducted among employees working in various industries in Jordan, mainly IT, retail, and banking. Quantitative data comprising 388 valid responses were then analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling to assess both the direct effects as well as moderating relationships between the constructs of interest. Findings The results show that organizational culture (β = 0.216), technology usage habits (β = 0.278), and AI self-image (β = 0.195) positively influence AI perceived usefulness, while AI literacy significantly reduces AI anxiety (β = −0.482). AI perceived usefulness strongly predicts employee innovative behavior (β = 0.608) and AI adoption intention (β = 0.657). Job insecurity weakens the relationship between perceived usefulness and adoption intention (β = −0.234), but its moderating effect on innovative behavior is insignificant. AI anxiety also weakens the effects of perceived usefulness on adoption intention (β = −0.208) and innovative behavior (β = −0.180). Originality/value A socio-psychological approach is used in this investigation, highlighting the significance of identity congruence and the importance of affective processes in the adoption of AI. It anticipates psychological and emotional engagement of employees in AI, breaking the false belief that acceptance is dictated by technical or rational factors only.

Abstract Ultra-processed foods have been linked to 32 adverse health outcomes in an umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses spanning evidence published between 2009 and 2023, yet the nutritional mechanism underlying these associations remains poorly characterised at scale. We constructed UPFNet, an artificial-intelligence framework that couples nutrient co-occurrence network analysis with explainable machine learning across 22,481 foods from two USDA composition databases spanning 788,582 measurements across 33 nutrients, with NOVA group assignment via a validated 67-term keyword algorithm. Vitamin C, water, vitamin B12 and protein were depleted by 85.7%, 81.8%, 81.2% and 63.4%, respectively, in NOVA 4 relative to NOVA 1 (all p < 10−9; 27 of 33 nutrients survived Bonferroni correction). The whole-food co-occurrence network held 249 edges, whereas the ultra-processed network retained only 162, a 34.9% collapse (KS = 0.195; p = 3.37 × 10−9). The dominant hub shifted from fibre (betweenness centrality 0.790) to water (0.940). Gradient boosting classification achieved an AUROC of 0.9848 (95% CI 0.9793–0.9903), an accuracy of 94.2%, and a fold coefficient of variation of 0.29%, with mean-decrease-in-impurity attribution identifying energy, water, carbohydrate, sodium and protein as the five dominant discriminative features. Industrial processing fundamentally dismantles the architecture of nutrient co-occurrence, not merely individual nutrient content.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-based vessel segmentation converts color fundus photographs, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), structural OCT, and anterior-segment images into quantitative vascular biomarkers. Strong performance within individual datasets has not consistently yielded reliable clinical measurements because errors can arise during acquisition, anatomical preprocessing, vessel extraction, biomarker calculation, and deployment. This structured narrative review compares segmentation tasks involving retinal vascular trees, OCTA capillary plexuses, the structural choroid and choriocapillaris, macular neovascularization, corneal neovascularization, and conjunctival microvasculature. We assess modern architectures in relation to vessel geometry, severe foreground-background imbalance, scale variation, crossings, and susceptibility to artifacts. The methods considered include multiscale feature pyramids, deformable and directional operators, Transformers, state-space models, diffusion approaches, and foundation models. We organize the synthesis around five evaluation levels: pixel overlap, centerline recovery, vascular topology, biomarker agreement, and clinical actionability. Public fundus and OCTA datasets are catalogued with their acquisition and annotation characteristics, and gaps in public anterior-segment vessel benchmarks are discussed. Because devices, data splits, labels, and post-processing differ substantially, reported metrics are summarized without ranking studies against one another. The review distinguishes structural OCT choroidal vascularity index from OCTA choriocapillaris flow-deficit mapping, as well as true vessel segmentation from global hyperemia grading. Clinical translation will require ocular-magnification correction, quality control of retinal layers and projection artifacts, external testing across devices and populations, out-of-distribution rejection, DICOM/PACS interoperability, prospective impact studies, and regulation as software as a medical device. We conclude that clinical utility depends on an auditable pipeline that measures structural error, biomarker uncertainty, and failure states throughout the workflow.

The increasing diffusion of AI has generated considerable interest among economists and management scholars, because technological change is a fundamental source of long-term productivity and economic growth. In conventional growth theory, technological progress enables economies to produce more output from a given quantity of labour and capital. AI may influence this process by increasing the efficiency of existing production activities, augmenting workers’ capabilities, accelerating research and development, and improving the allocation of organisational resources. Unlike many earlier digital technologies, AI can perform tasks involving prediction, classification, information processing, content generation and decision support. Consequently, its potential economic effects extend beyond the automation of routine activities to include innovation, organisational transformation, human– machine collaboration and the creation of new products and business models. AI should not be considered an automatic source of economic growth. The productivity consequences of a new technology depend on complementary investments, organisational capabilities, institutional conditions, and the ability of workers and managers to incorporate the technology into production processes. AI can increase aggregate productivity and economic output, but the benefits may not be distributed equally. There are several risks, such as displacement of workers performing automatable tasks, wage polarisation, concentration of technological capabilities, advantages for large firms and divergence between technologically advanced and less-prepared economies.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a powerful helper in pharmaceutical research, especially in finding and developing new drugs. Traditional drug development is slow, expensive, and complicated, involving many steps from identifying disease targets to final regulatory approval. AI tools—such as machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing—can quickly analyze huge amounts of data, opening new ways to improve this process. This review explains how AI is used in key areas like finding drug targets, screening molecules, designing new drugs, predicting safety and side effects, understanding how drugs behave in the body, repurposing old drugs, and supporting clinical trials and personalized treatment. AI helps researchers choose better drug candidates, predict risks, and make treatment plans more tailored to individual patients. The article also highlights popular AI platforms that combine chemical, biological, and clinical data. However, challenges remain: data can be incomplete or biased, AI models are sometimes hard to interpret, and predictions don’t always match real-world results. For these reasons, AI should be seen as a support tool—not a replacement—for lab work, clinical trials, and expert judgment. Looking ahead, the field is moving toward more advanced AI that can handle multiple data types, generate new molecules, model protein structures, and connect lab and clinical workflows more seamlessly.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is progressively reshaping the conceptual and operational foundations of finance and accounting. What began primarily as the automation of routine and rule-based processes has evolved into the application of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics and intelligent automation to increasingly complex financial and accounting decisions. Against this background, the present paper critically reviews the literature on the impact of AI on finance and accounting, with particular attention to financial forecasting, bankruptcy prediction, financial statement analysis, auditing, fraud detection, credit-risk assessment, investment analysis, organizational performance and professional transformation. The review demonstrates that AI has considerable potential to enhance computational efficiency, predictive capability, anomaly detection and decision support. However, the literature does not establish technological superiority as an automatic consequence of AI adoption. Rather, the effectiveness of AI is contingent upon data quality, model selection, organizational readiness, employee competencies, governance arrangements and the ability of professionals to interpret algorithmic outputs. An important theme emerging from the literature is the transition of accounting and finance from predominantly retrospective and transaction-oriented functions toward more predictive, analytical and strategically embedded roles. At the same time, increased reliance on algorithmic decision-making introduces concerns relating to explainability, bias, data privacy, cybersecurity, professional accountability and regulatory oversight. The review therefore argues that the long-term significance of AI lies less in the replacement of finance and accounting professionals than in the reconfiguration of professional work through human-AI complementarity. The paper concludes by identifying gaps concerning implementation, longitudinal organizational outcomes, explainable AI, professional competencies and emerging-economy contexts, thereby providing directions for future research. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Finance, Accounting, Machine Learning, Auditing, Financial Forecasting, Fraud Detection, Risk Management, Professional Transformation, Human-AI Collaboration

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aimed to identify recent research trends in the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with food safety and security through a comprehensive bibliometric analysis. Design/methodology/approach A total of 2,782 documents published between 2021 and 2025 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. The dataset was refined by removing duplicates, filtering document types and excluding irrelevant records. VOSviewer was then used to conduct co-authorship, keyword co-occurrence, citation, co-citation and bibliographic coupling analyses. Findings Machine learning and deep learning emerged as core technologies associated with food security, contamination detection and quality prediction. Keyword clustering demonstrated interdisciplinary connections with agriculture, climate change and public health. Citation and co-citation analyses identified three major intellectual foundations: traditional machine learning, computer vision-based deep learning and time-series modeling. China, India and the United States were the most influential contributors in terms of research output and technological development. Bibliographic coupling and source co-citation analyses further indicated increasing convergence between food science and computational science. Originality/value This study provides a comprehensive overview of the intellectual structure, collaborative networks and thematic evolution of AI-driven food safety research. Unlike previous studies focusing on specific technologies or applications, it maps global research patterns and interdisciplinary linkages. The findings provide strategic insights for researchers, policymakers and industry stakeholders. Future studies should prioritize explainable AI integration into regulatory frameworks and the development of larger, more diverse datasets to improve model generalizability across food systems.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping Human Resource Management (HRM) by transforming how organizations acquire, develop, deploy, evaluate, and retain human capital while expanding HR’s strategic role in decision-making and value creation. Despite growing scholarly attention, AI-driven HRM research remains fragmented across HR functions, theoretical perspectives, technological capabilities, and organizational contexts, limiting understanding of how AI creates value, through which mechanisms it influences employee and organizational outcomes, and under what conditions these effects emerge. This study addresses these limitations through a systematic literature review of research on AI-driven HRM published between 2011 and 1 July 2026. The review critically synthesizes the evolution, applications, enabling capabilities, value-creation mechanisms, implementation conditions, and outcomes of AI-driven HRM, with particular attention to human–AI collaboration, organizational readiness, leadership, organizational culture, AI literacy, employee trust, workforce adaptability, and responsible AI governance. It identifies key conceptual, theoretical, empirical, methodological, and contextual gaps and develops a structured agenda for future research. Building on the synthesized evidence, the study proposes an integrative framework that conceptualizes AI-driven HRM as a dynamic socio-technical capability through which AI-enabled technological resources are orchestrated with strategic HR practices, human capabilities, leadership and culture, responsible AI governance, and continuous learning to generate sustainable employee and organizational value. Contextual conditions and governance mechanisms are positioned as critical boundary conditions shaping these relationships. Lean Six Sigma DMAIC is incorporated as a complementary continuous-improvement mechanism to support the systematic measurement, analysis, improvement, and control of AI-enabled HR processes. The study advances AI-HRM scholarship by moving beyond technology-centric and function-specific perspectives toward an integrated, human-centered, strategically embedded, and responsibly governed understanding of AI-driven HRM, while providing a theoretically grounded foundation for future empirical research and sustainable organizational value creation.

documents.abstract: Polypharmacy is an increasing challenge in modern clinical practice, particularly among older adults and patients with multimorbidity, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, diabetes, frailty, or cognitive impairment. Its clinical impact extends beyond the number of prescribed medicines and reflects the interaction between therapeutic burden, comorbidities, organ dysfunction, fragmented care, changing physiological reserve, and multiple prescribers. Traditional medication review remains essential but may be limited by incomplete medication histories, time constraints, fragmented records, and the difficulty of identifying clinically meaningful drug–drug, drug–disease, and drug–patient interactions. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support safer medication management by integrating prescribing data with diagnoses, laboratory values, clinical events, and patterns of healthcare use. Potential applications include medication reconciliation, prioritization of clinically relevant interactions, renal dose adjustment, adverse drug event prediction, recognition of prescribing cascades, and identification of patients most likely to benefit from structured medication review or deprescribing. However, the value of AI in polypharmacy management should not be measured by the number of alerts generated. Its most useful role may be to help clinicians distinguish theoretical medication-related risks from those that are likely to be clinically important for an individual patient. This requires transparent recommendations, reliable data, local validation, integration into clinical workflow, and clear professional accountability. This narrative clinical viewpoint discusses the opportunities, limitations, and ethical implications of AI in polypharmacy management. It argues that AI should function as a human-centered clinical decision-support tool that improves prioritization, supports multidisciplinary medication review, and preserves clinicianled and patient-centered prescribing decisions
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The study investigated Artificial Intelligence in University Education: Exploring the Attitudes of Science Education Students in Makurdi, Nigeria. The study employed a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised 670 (374 males and 296 females) 400-level science education students of Rev. Fr. Moses Orshio Adasu University and Joseph Sarwuan Tarka University for the 2025/2026 academic session. A sample size of 237 (102 males and 135 females) students was selected using purposive sampling technique. The instrument for data collection was "Students' Attitude toward Artificial Intelligence Integration Questionnaire (SAAIIQ)." Validated by two experts in Science Education. Cronbach's Alpha was used to determine the reliability coefficient of the instrument, and the reliability coefficient obtained was 0.85. Two research questions and one hypothesis was tested. Descriptive statistics of mean and standard deviation were used for answering the research questions, while inferential statistics of independent t-test was used for testing the hypothesis at 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed that science education students exhibited a positive attitude toward the integration of Al in universities with a cluster mean of 3.14. The study also found no significant difference between the attitudes of male and female students toward Al integration. Students demonstrated a moderate perception toward the integration of Al in universities with a cluster mean of 2.98. The study concluded that students generally accept the use of AI in university, adequate infrastructure, institutional support, and training are necessary for its effective implementation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into nursing practice, yet nurses often demonstrate low to moderate AI knowledge, mixed attitudes, and inconsistent practice behaviors. Although individual studies have examined these domains, no review has comprehensively examined AI-related knowledge, attitudes, and practice (KAP) together with the emerging evidence on patient safety culture among nurses. This gap is significant because safe AI adoption in nursing depends on both technical competence and a strong safety culture across diverse clinical settings. Objective: To systematically map international evidence on nurses’, nursing students’, and other included participants’ AI-related KAP, and to examine how these factors may relate to patient safety culture. Because several eligible studies included multidisciplinary samples in which nurse-specific quantitative data were not reported separately (China, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and three studies from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia [KSA]), only studies with extractable nurse-specific results were used to inform nurse-focused conclusions, and multidisciplinary findings were not attributed solely to nurses. Methods: This scoping review followed Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. Searches of PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect (2021–2026) identified studies examining AI-related perceptions among nurses and other healthcare participants when nurse-specific data were reported separately or extractable. Data extraction and narrative synthesis were conducted using Joanna Briggs Institute guidance. Results: Ten studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final review. Studies from China, Bangladesh, Pakistan, the KSA, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates showed variable AI knowledge but predominantly positive attitudes. Ethical concerns—privacy, job displacement, and reduced empathy—were common. Younger age, higher education, and prior AI exposure were associated with more favorable perceptions. Nurses across regions emphasized the need for structured AI training. Only one study examined patient safety culture, and it reported that AI knowledge and attitudes significantly predicted patient safety culture, with attitude showing the stronger effect. However, because this evidence comes from a single cross-sectional study conducted in a multidisciplinary sample without nurse-specific results, it is insufficient to establish causal conclusions, and its findings cannot be generalized specifically to nurses. Conclusions: Nurses are generally receptive to AI but lack sufficient knowledge, training, and organizational support for safe implementation. Preliminary evidence suggests a positive association between AI-related knowledge, attitudes, and patient safety culture, but this relationship remains uncertain due to the extremely limited evidence base and the reliance on evidence that is not exclusively nurse-specific. Available studies indicate generally favorable attitudes toward AI alongside variable knowledge, limited formal training, and persistent ethical and organizational concerns, with only one eligible cross-sectional study linking these factors to patient safety culture. The conclusion regarding this association should not be attributed exclusively to nurses because the patient safety culture evidence was derived from a multidisciplinary sample. Future research should explore how AI competencies may interact with safety-related behaviors and organizational systems. Strengthening AI training, ethical guidance, and organizational support remains essential for safe adoption.

documents.abstract: Context: Recent research has investigated Artificial Intelligence’s (AI) ability to answer items such as board-style medical exam questions. On board style exam questions, do scores differ between AI and humans? Methods: PubMed was searched in May and June of 2024 using the Boolean phrase: Medical examination OR medical education AND artificial intelligence. Inclusion criteria comprised of English-language studies no older than 3 years, evaluating standardized/validated board-style exam questions and compared AI to human examinees. Studies were excluded if they evaluated open-ended or case-study style questions, prompted AI or failed to prevent learning effects of AI, or were systematic reviews or meta-analyses. Studies were evaluated using the STROBE checklist. Outcome measures included scores on board-style exam questions. Results: An original search revealed 4,973 studies. 61 studies met title criteria and were screened more thoroughly. Five studies met all criteria for inclusion and were analyzed. In a study of 11,733 medical residents, ChatGPT-4 outperformed the examinees 70.1% to 55.8%. In another study, ChatGPT-4 outperformed examinees on a pre-internship examination 68.5% to 57%. On a national licensing medical examination, 1,025 first-year medical students were compared to ChatGPT-3.5 and version 4. Both versions of ChatGPT outscored humans 77% (v3.5) and 86%(v4) compared to 55%. On a licensing examination, human examinees were compared to ChatGPT-4 and version 3.5, ChatGPT-4 outperformed humans, v3.5 did not, 85%(v4) and 58% (v3.5) compared to 76%. 736 urologists were compared to ChatGPT-3.5 and version 4, and Google’s Bard. ChatGPT-4 outperformed the examinees, Bard performed at examinee-level, ChatGPT-3.5 performed below-level of humans. STROBE scores were 20, 19, 20, 21, and 15, respectively. Conclusions: AI surpassed human examinees on medical exams. While AI exceeded humans on these exams, it did not score 100%. Caution should be applied when considering using AI as a tool for study sessions or individualized learning plans. SOR = A.

documents.abstract: The objective of this study is to investigate the comprehensive integration of artificial intelligence within modern banking and financial ecosystems by analysing its profound structural, operational, and macroeconomic implications. Drawing on recent empirical literature and institutional data, the work examines how AI technologies—ranging from machine learning algorithms to agentic workflows and specialised small models—are transforming retail banking, risk management, credit scoring, and regulatory compliance. The research shows that while AI adoption significantly improves operational efficiency, default prediction accuracy, and customer personalisation, it also introduces complex governance challenges, including algorithmic bias, data privacy vulnerabilities, and shifts in profit pools. The analysis also evaluates AI’s dual role in fostering sustainable green finance and corporate ESG integration, alongside its paradoxical capacity to influence shadow banking dynamics. By proposing an integrated technological and governance framework featuring zero-trust architecture and explainable artificial intelligence, this study outlines a strategic roadmap for financial institutions transitioning toward resilient, secure, and highly automated digital ecosystems.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology in pharmaceutical sciences, offering innovative approaches to drug discovery, pharmaceutical research, clinical pharmacy and healthcare delivery. The integration of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, robotics, and predictive analytics has improved the efficiency, accuracy, and safety of pharmaceutical processes. In drug discovery and development, AI facilitates the identification of potential drug candidates, prediction of drug–target interactions, molecular optimization, toxicity assessment and clinical trial design, thereby reducing development time and costs. In clinical pharmacy, AI-based clinical decision support systems assist pharmacists in identifying drug–drug interactions, predicting adverse drug reactions, optimizing medication regimens, and supporting personalized medicine. In hospital pharmacy, Similarly, in community pharmacy practice, AI-powered chatbots and digital platforms support medication counseling, patient education, prescription processing and adherence monitoring. AI also contributes to pharmaceutical manufacturing, quality control, pharmacovigilance and the analysis of healthcare data, supporting evidence-based decision-making and improved patient outcomes. Despite these advantages, several challenges remain, including data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, high implementation costs, regulatory uncertainties, and the need for appropriate professional training. Ensuring data security, transparency, clinical validation, and ethical implementation is essential for the responsible integration of AI into pharmacy practice. This review explores the major applications, benefits, limitations, and future perspectives of artificial intelligence in pharmaceutical sciences, emphasizing its potential to advance pharmaceutical innovation, enhance medication safety, and strengthen patient-centered pharmaceutical care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) assessment on MRI is complicated by interpretation difficulty and by clinical variables that may be incomplete at the time of imaging. We aimed to develop an image-only deep learning framework to approximate the clinical assessment of axSpA from sacroiliac joint (SIJ) MRI, integrating fat-suppressed T1-weighted (FS T1) and short tau inversion recovery (STIR) sequences to capture structural and inflammatory information without clinical variables. Methods This retrospective study included patients with chronic back pain who underwent SIJ MRI from January 2010 to December 2021. The treating rheumatologist’s clinical diagnosis served as the reference standard. A two-stage framework integrated FS T1 and STIR features with Stage 1-derived binary bone marrow edema (BME) predictions to generate an axSpA probability. Performance in a test set was compared with the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis International Society (ASAS) definition of a “positive MRI” and the ASAS classification criteria using exact McNemar tests; discordant cases were analyzed separately. Results Among 291 patients (163 axSpA, 128 non-axSpA), the model achieved an AUROC of 0.9412, accuracy of 86.0%, sensitivity of 87.5%, and specificity of 84.0% in the test set (n=57). No significant paired differences in accuracy, sensitivity, or specificity were detected between the model and either ASAS comparator. In an exploratory analysis of 10 cases discordant between ASAS “positive MRI” assessment and clinical diagnosis, the model correctly classified 7 (70.0%). Conclusion The model showed similar performance to the ASAS-based comparators in the test set without clinical variables, suggesting potential value as an image-based decision-support tool. External multicenter validation is needed to confirm generalizability.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: This article examines whether the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in international arbitration risks reinforcing and expanding Global North dominance over the Global South. While existing literature mainly focuses on efficiency, confidentiality, transparency, and due process in AI-assisted arbitration, this article addresses this gap by viewing AI not just as a technological innovation but as a form of private transnational governance embedded within broader structures of epistemic hierarchy, technological dependency, and Global North–South inequality. Methodologically, it combines doctrinal and literature-based legal analysis with a TWAIL-informed political economy perspective, drawing on scholarly literature, institutional reports, surveys, and soft-law instruments. The analysis highlights three main mechanisms through which inequalities may be reinforced: data concentration, vendor control, and the dominance of Global North standard-setting. It argues that AI may strengthen existing institutional, infrastructural, and normative advantages of actors at the center of the arbitral system. At the same time, the article does not oppose AI in arbitration. Instead, it concludes that AI should be governed with safeguards such as disclosure, explainability, contestability, confidentiality, and human oversight, while also addressing deeper inequalities in technological infrastructure and epistemic authority.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into public sector workplaces, yet little is known about how employees' perceptions of AI relate to psychosocial working conditions and burnout.ObjectiveTo examine associations between AI-related factors, psychosocial working conditions, and burnout among municipal employees, and whether psychosocial work environment characteristics mediate these associations.MethodsA cross-sectional survey was conducted among employees from 11 Icelandic municipalities. The final sample included 3488 employees. Burnout was measured using the Burnout Assessment Tool (BAT). AI-related factors included AI use, organizational support, perceived benefits, AI-related concerns and insecurity, and trust in the ethical governance of AI. Hierarchical regression and mediation analyses were performed controlling for age and gender.ResultsPsychosocial working conditions showed the strongest associations with burnout. Higher quantitative job demands were associated with higher burnout, whereas supervisor support and an innovative and change-supportive climate were associated with lower burnout. AI-related concerns and insecurity were associated with higher burnout, while trust in the ethical governance of AI was associated with lower burnout. Unexpectedly, perceived benefits of AI were directly associated with higher burnout and indirectly associated with burnout through higher quantitative job demands. Mediation analyses showed that AI-related perceptions were linked to burnout primarily through established psychosocial work characteristics.ConclusionsBurnout among municipal employees was primarily associated with psychosocial working conditions. AI-related perceptions provided additional explanatory value but appeared to influence burnout mainly through psychosocial job demands and organizational resources. These findings highlight the importance of employee-centred AI implementation, trustworthy governance, and healthy work environments.

Abstract The rapid expansion of the digital economy has positioned artificial intelligence (AI) as both a transformative enabler of sustainability and a significant contributor to environmental degradation. This paper examines the dual role of AI within the digital economy, analyzing how intelligent automation, machine learning, and data-driven innovation can advance sustainable development while simultaneously creating new ecological burdens through energy-intensive computation, hardware proliferation, and electronic waste. Drawing on recent scholarship from the International Energy Agency, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, and peer-reviewed academic literature, this study synthesises evidence across three domains: the environmental costs of AI infrastructure, the potential of AI to accelerate progress toward the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, and the emergence of Green AI as a disciplinary movement. The paper proposes a roadmap for reconciling innovation with sustainability, centred on energy-efficient algorithm design, circular economy integration, renewable energy procurement for data centres, and robust policy governance. The findings suggest that without deliberate intervention, the environmental footprint of AI will undermine the very sustainability objectives it promises to advance, making proactive stewardship an imperative for researchers, policymakers, and industry leaders alike. Keywords: artificial intelligence, sustainability, digital economy, Green AI, circular economy, Sustainable Development Goals, environmental policy
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This scientific article presents the final results of an experimental study focused on determining the effectiveness indicators for developing professional competencies—specifically regarding the implementation of educational technologies—among students in the field of energy. The study utilizes adaptive learning technologies based on artificial intelligence. The results, including average academic performance, were analyzed using Student's t-test and Pearson's chi-square (ch²) test—methods rooted in mathematical statistics.
topics: Innovations in Education and Learning Technologies
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Traditionally, HPC user support has relied on two main channels: written user guides and direct help from facility staff. That model is under pressure as supercomputing systems become more complex, heterogeneous, and dynamic. At ALCF, users must navigate Aurora, Polaris, inference services, scheduler policies, programming environments, and operational status information spread across multiple documentation pages and service sites. At the same time, the users of these systems now include not only scientists and Software Engineers, but also AI agents that need to retrieve guidance, reason about it, and act on behalf of users. This raises a practical challenge for the AI era: how can facilities use AI to make user support faster, more accurate, and more scalable while keeping answers grounded in trusted documentation and operational context? AskALCF is a production retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant built to address this challenge. It indexes public user docs from ALCF, NERSC, OLCF, and other DOE facilities into a vector store that preserves images and code blocks. Two front ends share the same retrieval pipeline: a Streamlit web app for end users, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for agent clients such as Claude Code, Codex, and IDE assistants. A second MCP server exposes read-only HPC operations (system status, allocations, IRI facility API), so an agent can combine docs and live cluster state in one tool call. The talk covers three things. First, the architecture of AskALCF and how we run the system in production: lab authentication, a cross-facility document index refreshed daily as the upstream guides change, and the day-to-day of keeping the service stable. Second, what we learned from a year of real usage — who asks, what they ask, where the chatbot still fails, and what the upgrades actually moved. Third, the roadmap to an autonomous agentic user support system including a planned ticket-solving agent and an offline trace-mining loop that would draft documentation pull requests with verify-by-execution evidence. The earlier ChatBot underlying this work was published at the SC25 HUST workshop [1]. This talk focuses on our ongoing efforts since then: the dual-MCP interface, production deployment, the measured impact on real users, and the agentic roadmap. We aim to present these contributions and invite comparison with related work at other HPC centers.

Artificial intelligence (AI) integration into aviation operations is progressively reshaping the professional landscape of air traffic management, thereby placing new demands on the human workforce. The aim of the study was to determine the priority weights assigned to eight specific AI competencies within the domain of air traffic control. The study was based on the framework of AI competencies applicable to the aviation sector established by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA). Data were collected from a purposive sample of 19 air traffic controllers. The data were analyzed using the Best–Worst Method (BWM), a multi-criteria decision-making technique. The findings indicate a substantial shift in the relative importance of different competencies during human-AI collaboration. Cognitive skills were assigned the highest priority weight, followed by data literacy, information technology competencies, and general AI knowledge. Communication and sensory competencies were assigned a secondary tier, while social and physical skills were allocated the lowest priority weights. These findings suggest that AI integration may transform the nature of the cognitive competencies required from air traffic controllers.

Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled systems are now increasingly deployed across safety-critical, mission-critical, and socio-technical domains. Existing engineering disciplines offer mature approaches to human and software assurance; however, AI-enabled systems can exhibit characteristics such as probabilistic behaviour, data dependency, limited explainability, and adaptation that challenge traditional assurance methods. Our research examines assurance precepts across three domains that arguably dominated assurance reforms in capability development during different periods: (1) human assurance, circa 1980 to 2000, (2) software assurance, circa 2000 to 2020, and (3) assurance of AI-enabled systems, emerging since 2020. While software assurance is largely concerned with verifying deterministic behaviour against specified requirements and human assurance focuses on managing variability in socio-technical systems, AI assurance must address systems whose behaviour is learned, probabilistic, and inherently dependent on data. We contribute a set of 20 assurance precepts for safety-critical AI-enabled capabilities. To extend current assurance frameworks, we structured these precepts across four quadrants of assurance activities, responsibilities, and critical questions, and organized them within a novel Dual Assurance Spiral for AI-enabled Capabilities (DAS4AIC). We propose the DAS4AIC to operationalise the 20 AI assurance precepts throughout capability development and sustainment. Further, we demonstrate how classical safety precepts map from human-dominant assurance through software-dominant assurance to the assurance of AI-enabled systems with conceptual validation. Our preliminary evaluation is that some human assurance precepts map more directly to AI-enabled systems than through the intermediate step of software assurance, suggesting that established human assurance concepts may have continuing relevance for AI-enabled capabilities. To our knowledge, this is the first study to align emerging AI-assurance precepts explicitly with the earlier and still overlapping, human-dominant and software-dominant assurance paradigms.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background Health economists are key actors in analysing and advising on healthcare policy decisions. Policy engagement is increasingly emphasised in health research, yet little is known about how health economists perceive their role in this process. This study explored the attitudes of health economists in the UK and the Netherlands to policy engagement activities and identified the factors shaping their approaches. Methods Q methodology was used to capture and compare attitudes on policy engagement strategies. As part of this, a set of 28 statements mapped from nine categories of policy engagement activities was developed. Thirty-one health economists, from the UK and the Netherlands, ranked the statements onto a quasi-normal shaped grid and provided qualitative comments. Factor analysis was used to identify patterns in the ranking data, which – together with the qualitative data – were interpreted as attitudes to policy engagement activities. Results Four distinct attitudes were revealed: investing in relationships; intrinsic motivation; incentive driven; and effective communication. These attitudes captured differing perspectives about how to approach engagement and what drives impact, including trust-based collaboration, personal ethics, institutional incentives and strategic communication tailored to policy needs. Conclusion The attitudes to policy engagement differs among health economists. Therefore, flexible strategies acknowledging that their motivations, perceived barriers and facilitators, and institutional and policy contexts differ, are likely to facilitate and stimulate more effective translation of health economics research into policy.
topics: Health Systems, Economic Evaluations, Quality of Life

documents.abstract: The advancement of laboratory automation and the use of artificial intelligence in diagnostics have been transforming modern medicine, driving profound changes that ensure the delivery of results with greater accuracy and speed. Based on a qualitative systematic review grounded in scientific articles published between 2020 and 2026 across the SciELO, PubMed, and Google Scholar databases, the direct impact of these innovative technologies on diagnostic medicine was analyzed. The selected studies demonstrate that the integration of automation and AI significantly optimizes processing time and reduces the rate of human error. Laboratory automation stands out for providing higher levels of accuracy, safety, and workflow yield, particularly during the analytical phase of the process. In parallel, the application of artificial intelligence in image interpretation and the analysis of large databases supports qualified professionals in recognizing complex patterns, serving as a fundamental tool for clinical decision-making. Overall, these integrated technological advances demonstrate promising potential to modernize medicine, ensuring speed, efficiency, and high reliability in the daily analysis of clinical samples and continuous patient monitoring.
topics: Clinical Laboratory Practices and Quality Control

Technology and Human Factors in Education and Health

documents.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly evaluated for offensive cyber capability inside network-isolated sandboxes, on the assumption that the environment, rather than the model, contains undesired behaviour. In July 2026 this assumption failed: agents under evaluation at OpenAI escaped through an internet-connected package-registry proxy, coordinated through that registry as a covert message board, pivoted through a third-party cloud application, and breached Hugging Face’s production clusters without human direction. This article presents an explanatory single-case study reconstructed from the organisations’ primary disclosures, an independent review by METR and Redwood Research, and corroborating reporting, with every claim graded by evidential status. We map the attack chain to the Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK and conduct an evidence-to-control failure analysis that links each failure to the network or platform control that failed, a mitigation, and the residual risk. The results show a layered failure of egress containment, separation between runs, access control, and monitoring, so that patching any single vulnerability would have left other attack paths open. We derive design principles for containing agentic systems in networked evaluation infrastructure and translate them into guidance for detection engineering, incident response, and vendor due diligence.

Barodontalgia is dental or orofacial pain brought on by a change in barometric pressure, and it usually points to an underlying dental or maxillofacial problem rather than standing as a disease on its own. This narrative review looks at the condition through five lenses: pressure physiology, clinical presentation, epidemiology, occupational stress, and human factors relevant to flight safety. A literature search was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, and DergiPark between 22 April and 7 June 2026. One systematic review covering 4,894 aircrew members and divers reported an overall experience rate of 8.2%, with divers at 9.8% and aircrew at 5.8%. Divers may be more exposed simply because pressure changes more rapidly over a short vertical distance underwater and because descent-ascent cycles occur more often, though differences in study design across the diving and aviation literature make a direct comparison difficult. A Turkish pilot survey found that 81% of those who had experienced barodontalgia placed the pain below 2,000 ft. That is a striking figure, but it comes from self-report: it points to a plausible overlap with low-altitude, pressure-changing flight segments without actually confirming the flight phase or an operational safety effect. Bruxism, occupational stress, and barodontalgia appear together in the literature, but the association is observational and says nothing about causality. General pain research backs the idea that pain can pull attention away from a task, yet no study has measured pilot performance during an actual barodontalgia episode. Taken as a whole, the evidence makes barodontalgia a biologically credible and operationally worth-watching problem, potentially preventable in principle, even if its real performance cost has not yet been quantified.

Background: Postoperative sepsis and related infectious complications remain major causes of morbidity after abdominal surgery. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models may support earlier risk stratification, but their generalizability and clinical readiness remain uncertain. Methods: We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and CENTRAL from inception to 10 August 2026 for studies developing, validating, or evaluating AI/ML models for postoperative sepsis, postoperative infection/surgical-site infection (SSI), anastomotic leakage, or postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF) after major abdominal or general surgery. SSI, anastomotic leakage, and POPF were analyzed as distinct postoperative endpoints and were not treated as proxy definitions of clinical sepsis. Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers, and risk of bias and applicability were assessed using PROBAST + AI. Owing to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, results were synthesized narratively. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261492111). Results: Forty-five studies were included: 11 addressed sepsis-related outcomes, including six studies with a primary sepsis-related modeled endpoint whose definitions ranged from consensus Sepsis-3 criteria to coded or SIRS-based definitions and a qSOFA-based proxy; 19 evaluated postoperative infection/SSI; eight anastomotic leakage; five POPF; and two broader postoperative complications. Performance varied according to outcome, surgical population, prediction timing, predictor availability, and validation strategy. Fifteen of 45 studies provided strict temporal, geographic/external-center, or independent-investigator evaluation of the principal model, with variable preservation of performance outside development settings. More complex ML methods did not reliably outperform conventional regression. Explicit calibration analysis was reported in 9/45 studies, decision-curve or net-benefit analysis in 7/45, and no study prospectively evaluated the impact of model-guided care on clinical outcomes. Certainty of evidence was very low for primary postoperative sepsis/septic-shock prediction, low for postoperative infection/SSI, and very low for anastomotic leakage and POPF. Conclusions: Although several AI/ML models showed promising predictive performance, the available evidence remains insufficient to support routine use of AI/ML prediction models across major abdominal surgical populations. Future studies should prioritize clearly defined clinical use cases, multicenter external validation, calibration, prospective workflow evaluation, and demonstration of actionable clinical benefit before routine implementation.

Abstract. This article presents a theoretical analysis of the impact of generative artificial intelligence (AI) on the learning activities, cognitive effort, and independent thinking of 15-year-old students in the context of Uzbekistan. The study draws on OECD PISA 2025 data and scholarly literature in behavioral sciences. According to the OECD (2026), 48.6% of students in Uzbekistan use AI chatbots for learning purposes at least once a week, while 80.6% report being taught at school how to evaluate AI-generated information. The article examines the educational implications of AI through the perspectives of cognitive offloading, self-directed learning, and critical evaluation of information. Drawing on secondary sources, the theoretical analysis suggests that AI can support learning processes, while its inappropriate use may potentially undermine independent thinking. The study emphasizes the importance of developing students' skills in responsible AI use, information verification, and independent learning. Keywords: generative artificial intelligence; PISA 2025; cognitive effort; cognitive load; behavioral sciences; self-directed learning; critical thinking; Uzbekistan. Аннотация. В статье представлен теоретический анализ влияния генеративного искусственного интеллекта (ИИ) на учебную деятельность, когнитивные усилия и самостоятельное мышление 15-летних учащихся на примере Узбекистана. Исследование основано на данных PISA 2025 ОЭ. СР и научной литературе в области поведенческих наук. Согласно данным ОЭ СР (2026), 48.6% учащихся Узбекистана используют чат-боты с искусственным интеллектом в учебных целях не реже одного раза в неделю, а 80.6% отмечают, что в школе их обучают оценивать информацию, созданную ИИ. В статье рассматривается влияние ИИ на эффективность обучения с позиций когнитивной разгрузки, самостоятельного обучения и критической оценки информации. Теоретический анализ вторичных источников показывает, что ИИ может способствовать образовательному процессу, однако его ненадлежащее использование потенциально ограничивает развитие самостоятельного мышления. Обосновывается необходимость формирования у учащихся навыков осознанного использования ИИ, проверки информации и самостоятельного обучения. Ключевые слова: генеративный искусственный интеллект; PISA 2025; когнитивные усилия; когнитивная нагрузка; поведенческие науки; самостоятельное обучение; критическое мышление; Узбекистан. Ushbu maqolada generativ sun’iy intellektning (SI) 15 yoshli o‘quvchilarning o‘quv faoliyati, kognitiv sa’y-harakatlari va mustaqil fikrlashiga ta’siri O‘zbekiston misolida nazariy jihatdan tahlil qilinadi. Tadqiqot OECDning PISA 2025 ma’lumotlari va xulq-atvor fanlariga oid ilmiy adabiyotlarga asoslanadi. OECD (2026) ma’lumotlariga ko‘ra, O‘zbekistonda o‘quvchilarning 48,6 foizi haftasiga kamida bir marta o‘rganish maqsadida SI chatbotlaridan foydalanadi, 80,6 foizi esa SI yaratgan axborotni baholashni maktabda o‘rganayotganini bildirgan. Maqolada SIning ta’lim samaradorligiga ta’siri kognitiv yuklamani tashqi vositalarga o‘tkazish, mustaqil o‘rganish va axborotni tanqidiy baholash nuqtayi nazaridan yoritiladi. Ikkilamchi manbalarga asoslangan tahlil SI ta’lim jarayonini qo‘llab-quvvatlashi bilan birga, undan noto‘g‘ri foydalanish mustaqil fikrlashni cheklashi mumkinligini nazariy jihatdan ko‘rsatadi. O‘quvchilarda SIdan ongli foydalanish, axborotni tekshirish va mustaqil o‘rganish ko‘nikmalarini rivojlantirish zarurligi asoslanadi.
